Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
The people responsible have faced no consequences
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Body Shame' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile for a civilian-in-war-zone trauma unless there is some indication of bodily violation, injury, or humiliation. The other selected items center on injustice, impunity, hypervigilance, dissociative/fragmented memory, and avoidance, but provide no supporting context for body-focused shame, making this item stand out as clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: The Threat items emphasize pervasive current danger and hypervigilance (scanning exits, needing to stay alert at night), but the formulation specifically has Triggers → Threat inactive. In this profile, Triggers are concrete reminders such as car sounds and related media, yet the Threat items are generalized and not plausibly linked to those triggers; this makes the threat presentation feel disconnected from the trigger pattern.

vignette:
Minh Tran is a 74-year-old Vietnamese American man who has worked as a welder for most of his adult life, arriving in the United States as a refugee in the late 1970s after surviving the fall of Saigon and its brutal aftermath. He is married, lives in a modest home in a mid-sized city, and until recently continued part-time welding work at a small fabrication shop - a trade he had carried with him across oceans and decades. He presented for psychological assessment after his wife, increasingly alarmed by his deteriorating sleep and his habit of sitting alone in the dark after nightmares, insisted he speak with someone.

The events Minh describes - haltingly, and only in fragments - took place during a period of intense urban fighting in 1975, when he was a young man in his mid-twenties. He was caught in a district under bombardment, sheltering with several neighbours in a building that was struck. The sound of artillery and collapsing masonry was deafening. In the chaos that followed, he ran through open streets under fire, struggling to breathe through smoke and dust, watching people fall around him. He survived; others he had been sheltering with did not. The specific texture of that flight - the roar of vehicles, the open sky above exposed streets, the sensation of his lungs seizing - is precisely what makes his present environment so treacherous. When a car backfires or accelerates sharply near the fabrication shop where he still works, Minh's body responds before his mind can intervene: his chest tightens, his breathing becomes laboured, and he is pulled back into the streets of 1975 with a force that feels less like remembering and more like returning. The memory, when it comes, is fragmentary and strange to him - he describes it as though it happened to someone else, a story so extreme it is hard to believe it belongs to his own life, with whole sections simply missing, as if the tape had been cut.

Because the memory arrives in pieces and feels alien to him, Minh has never been able to construct a coherent account of what happened, and this incompleteness keeps the past perpetually unresolved and close. The fragmented quality of his recall means that certain sensory details - a rushing engine, the feeling of breathlessness, an image glimpsed on a television news broadcast showing bombed streets - carry disproportionate emotional charge, functioning as portals rather than reminders. When these triggers activate, Minh immediately redirects his attention, forcing himself to think about his welding work, the grain of metal under his hands, anything concrete and present. He avoids open spaces where he feels exposed - he no longer walks to the corner store and plans his routes to avoid wide intersections - and he refuses to talk with anyone, including his wife, about what he witnessed. These strategies have provided short-term relief but have ensured that the memory remains unprocessed and unintegrated, preserving its alien, fragmented character and allowing it to continue generating triggers without context or resolution.

Minh carries a corrosive sense of injustice that has deepened over five decades. He is certain that what was done to the civilians of his city was profoundly unfair, that those responsible have never been held to account, and - most painfully - that he bears some portion of blame himself, convinced that a different decision, a faster turn, might have saved the neighbours who died beside him. These appraisals are not abstract; they surface as a persistent, low-grade fury and a self-directed shame that together keep him in a state of chronic threat. He has come to believe that the world remains fundamentally dangerous and that he cannot afford to lower his guard, which manifests as difficulty concentrating at the welding bench, hypervigilance in any public setting, and an inability to fall asleep without first scanning the house. This sustained sense of threat, in turn, makes ordinary sounds - a car accelerating outside the shop, a door slamming - register as potential danger, feeding back into the cycle of intrusion and avoidance. His refusal to speak about the events has also allowed his self-blame to go unchallenged, hardening over years into something that feels like established fact rather than distorted appraisal.

What finally brought Minh to seek help was a moment at work: a delivery truck backfired in the yard outside the shop, and he dropped to the floor behind his workbench, unable to speak for several minutes while a younger colleague looked on. He said nothing to explain himself, drove home, and sat in the dark until morning. What he fears most is that he will never be free of it. What he hopes, though he can barely articulate it, is that someone might help him make the memory feel like his own.
